name: Fiji Hindi
confidence_why: Arms 1998, the only first-hand account of placement, puts stress on the penultimate syllable by default with weight-conditioned final and antepenultimate stress but calls the rule complex and in need of further research, while Moag 1977 only presupposes weak, even stress without saying where it falls, so nothing contradicts the rule but nothing confirms it either.

catalog_quote: NOTE: SHORT AND LONG VOWELS, In Hindi every vowel is either long or short. In this book long vowels are represented by double letters (aa, ii, uu, ai, au) while short vowels are represented by single letters (a, i, u, e, o). Short vowels are about half as long as long ones, and long vowels must be twice as long as the short ones. In English the length of time a vowel receives depends on the amount of stress it has. The quality of a vowel can change dramatically with varying stress in English as in the middle syllable of "emphasis" when it is changed to "emphatic". Fijian has long and short vowels, but their quality remains the same whatever the length. In Hindi both the length and quality of the vowels are unchanged by stress. Thus, the vowel in the first syllable of baRaa must be shorter and have a different sound from that in the last syllable. Likewise, the middle syllable of TamaaTa…

audit.recode_to: Quantity-sensitive (Hindi-type right-edge weight rule), hedged/non-strict: default penultimate stress; final stress when the final syllable is closed with a long vowel (superheavy); antepenultimate stress in polysyllables (final in disyllables) when the penult is open with a short vowel and the final is open. Source Arms 1998:3, with the author's own hedge ('seems largely predictable.. requires further research') carried into the caution field; keep Moag 1977:43-44/50-51 as the secondary quote on weak stress/no vowel reduction. strength of the evidence open-text (ANU text-layer PDF, CC BY-SA).
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the Moag 1977 passage is in the scanned file we hold at the stated lines/pages and in the official ANU open PDF downloaded now; one word differs ('distinct' not 'different'), otherwise verbatim, and it is indeed the book's only stress mention. (2) The deciding source is a pedagogical course note (1977) that presupposes stress but gives no rule. (3) Glottolog's own list contains Arms 1998 (Pacific Linguistics C-141:1-10), which I downloaded from ANU Open Research and read: p.3 states an explicit weight-conditioned placement rule with seven transcribed examples, framed as a correction/expansion of Moag, Siegel and Hobbs. That turns not determinable into a codable quantity-sensitive record, so the record is at-risk and should be reclassified (with Arms's hedge preserved). Siegel 1975 (held) and Siegel 1992 (downloaded) are silent; Prasad 2016 (USP MA thesis) and Siegel 1987 (CUP) could not be reach

sources.quote: 'Stress seems largely predictable in Fiji Hindi, although the rule is complex and the matter requires further research. Stress most often occurs on the penultimate syllable: (4)a. [paˈsina] 'sweat' b. [ˈgobʰi] 'cabbage' c. [ˈmarɩs] 'he hit'. However, it occurs on the final syllable if it is a closed syllable with a long vowel: (5)a. [bɩsˈwas] 'belief' b. [məjˈbut] 'strong'.
